stories.headline: Central team to visit districts affected by Murasu cyclone
stories.title: Central team to visit districts affected by Murasu cyclone
stories.summary: The team is scheduled to inspect four cyclone-affected districts of Palnadu, Bapatla, Eluru and East Godavari
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: After touring the districts affected by Cyclone Arnab, the Central team is visiting Andhra Pradesh again to tour the districts affected by Cyclone Murasu to assess the damage.

According to a release issued by the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, a seven-member Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT), led by Chittaranjan Das, Joint Secretary, Union Ministry of Home Affairs, will tour four cyclone-affected districts of Palnadu, Bapatla, Eluru and East Godavari.

In a release, APSDMA Managing Director Prakhar Jain said the Union government had appointed the same team, which was deputed to assess the damage caused by Arnab, to evaluate the losses resulting from Murasu as well.
The team will split into two groups during the field visits.
On Friday, the first team will visit Bapatla district, while the second team will tour Eluru district.
On Saturday, the first team will visit Palnadu and the second team will inspect the damage in East Godavari district.
The team is also likely to meet Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu on Sunday.

The seven-member team comprises Prashant Armorikar, Additional Development Commissioner, Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare; Rekha Rani Kollu, Superintending Engineer, Central Water Commission, Ministry of Jal Shakti; Himalaya Garg, Assistant Director, Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance; Shashank Shekhar Rai, Executive Engineer, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways; Alok Jawahar, Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Rural Development; Pranay Garg, Deputy Director, Ministry of Power; and S.V.S.P. Sharma, Scientist ‘SF’, National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), ISRO.

stories.headline: As winter sets in, LoC residents seek construction of bunkers
stories.title: As winter sets in, LoC residents seek construction of bunkers
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 12: With winter setting in across Kashmir, residents living along the Line of Control (LoC) in border areas have renewed their demand for the construction of underground community bunkers, saying the absence of adequate protective shelters continues to leave hundreds of families vulnerable in the event of cross-border shelling. Residents of border villages in Uri, Karnah, Keran, Machil and Gurez, among other vulnerable areas of north Kashmir, said that despite repeated assurances and discussions about improving civilian safety, several families still lack access to safe shelters near their homes. They said the onset of winter has added to their concerns, particularly as harsh weather conditions, snowfall and difficult road connectivity could make evacuation and movement to safer locations challenging during an emergency. “If shelling happens, where will we go? We cannot leave our homes and families every time there is tension along the border. We need underground bunkers in our villages so that people can take shelter immediately,” said Lal Hussain Kohli, a resident of Charunda village along LoC in Uri. They said the experience of previous ceasefire violations and cross-border shelling had exposed the vulnerability of border communities, with families often forced to rush towards safer locations without adequate protection. Residents said women, children, elderly people and patients were particularly at risk during such situations. They added that many households are located close to the LoC, leaving people with very little time to move to safer places when firing begins. “We have children and elderly family members at home. During shelling, it becomes difficult to move everyone to a safe place, especially at night and during winter. Every village should have properly constructed community bunkers within easy reach,” Tahir Ahmad, a local of Kupwara village said. The demand comes amid repeated concerns raised by residents of the Uri sector in Baramulla district, where several villages have experienced the impact of cross-border firing over the years. In villages such as Charunda, Garkote, Nambla, Kalgai, Salamabad, Ramgai, Kamalkote and Nowpora, residents have previously highlighted gaps in the availability and condition of protective shelters. Some residents have also raised concerns over the condition of existing bunkers, saying that a few structures are either inadequate or require repairs to make them usable during emergencies. They said the government should undertake a fresh assessment of all border villages across Kupwara, Baramulla and Bandipora districts to identify areas where bunkers are urgently required. Residents have also demanded that construction should not remain confined to villages that have witnessed recent shelling, arguing that all vulnerable settlements along the LoC should be covered under a comprehensive protection plan. “The construction of underground bunkers, along with proper ventilation, lighting, seating and other basic facilities, should be prioritised before the peak winter months,” said Hashim Ahmad, a local of Kamalkote sector. Locals of Karnah have further urged the administration to ensure that existing shelters are regularly inspected and maintained so that they remain accessible and functional whenever required. They have appealed to the district administrations to take up the issue on priority and carry out the work whenever necessary.

stories.headline: AIP reviews organisational expansion, seeks early verdict on Er Rashid’s bail
stories.title: AIP reviews organisational expansion, seeks early verdict on Er Rashid’s bail
stories.summary: SRINAGAR, Nov 12: The Awami Itihaad Party (AIP) on Thursday held an Executive Committee meeting in Srinagar to review its organisational activities, membership drive and plans for expanding its presence across Jammu and Kashmir. The meeting was chaired by Party Vice Chairman Advocate G. N. Shaheen and attended by General Secretary (Organisation) Prince Parveez, General Secretary Nazir Ahmad Khan, Chief Spokesperson Inam Un Nabi, State Secretary Sheikh Ashiq, MLA Langate Sheikh Khursheed and senior party leaders Peerzada Firdous Ahmad Baba, Mir Nazir Ahmad, Parvez Ahmad Bhat and Advocate Dawood Ahmad. The committee expressed concern over the continued incarceration of party president and Member of Parliament Engineer Rashid. Taking note of the Delhi High Court having reserved its judgment on his regular bail application, the members hoped that the verdict would be delivered at the earliest, enabling him to resume his public responsibilities. The meeting also reviewed the ongoing membership drive across Jammu and Kashmir. Party members expressed satisfaction over the response, describing the growing interest in joining AIP as an indication of its expanding organisational reach. Detailed discussions were held on strengthening the party structure, improving coordination at different levels and expanding its organisational presence, particularly in the Jammu Province. The committee reiterated its commitment to grassroots outreach, organisational consolidation and building the party's presence across all regions of Jammu and Kashmir.

stories.summary: According to the Income Tax Department’s instructions dated May 11, 1994, a married woman can possess up to 500 grams of gold, an unmarried woman up to 250 grams, and a man up to 100 grams. The case was sought to be dismissed on this basis.

stories.headline: India's Journey of Discovery and Innovation in Space
stories.title: India's Journey of Discovery and Innovation in Space
stories.summary: BEYOND THE SKY Space has always inspired human curiosity. From observing the stars to developing spacecraft, generations have sought to understand the universe and humanity's place within it. Today, advances in scientific research and technology are making it possible to explore space in ways once considered beyond reach. India is now an active part of this wider journey of discovery, with its space programme entering an important new phase. India's early space research began with modest facilities and ambitious scientific goals. On 21 November 1963, a research rocket carrying instruments to study the upper atmosphere was launched from Thumba in Kerala. India's first indigenous sounding rocket followed in 1967. Such rockets carry scientific instruments into the atmosphere to collect information. These early initiatives helped develop the knowledge and experience needed for a long-term space programme. Vikram Sarabhai, recognised as the father of India's space programme, believed that space technology could help address practical needs on Earth. His vision placed importance on communication, education, weather forecasting and the responsible use of scientific knowledge. That approach continues to influence the development of space technology. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has developed rockets and satellites that support communication, navigation, weather forecasting and early warnings of natural disasters. Its scientific missions have also contributed to the understanding of the Moon, Mars and the Sun. Chandrayaan-3 reached the Moon's southern high-latitude region on 23 August 2023, and its Pragyan rover conducted scientific studies on the lunar surface. Mangalyaan entered Mars orbit in September 2014, while Aditya-L1 reached its observing position in January 2024 to study the Sun. The space sector is also seeing growing participation from private Indian companies, which are contributing to the development of launch vehicles, satellites, engines and space-based services. This wider participation is creating opportunities for engineers, scientists, researchers and young entrepreneurs. Among the companies working in this field is Skyroot Aerospace, founded in Hyderabad in 2018. In November 2022, its Vikram-S rocket completed a suborbital test flight, demonstrating its rocket technology without placing a satellite into orbit. On 18 July 2026, the company's Vikram-1 made its maiden orbital launch, placing two satellites, Skyroot's SCOPE and Grahaa Space's SOLARAS S3, into low Earth orbit. An orbital launch, on the other hand, gives a satellite the speed and direction needed to continue travelling around Earth. These missions marked important stages in the development of Skyroot's launch vehicles. Agnikul Cosmos, based in Chennai, is developing small rockets designed to carry satellites. In May 2024, it tested Agnibaan SOrTeD using a single-piece engine made through 3D printing, a process in which an object is built layer by layer from a digital design. The flight was a suborbital technology test. Such experiments demonstrate how research, engineering and careful testing help turn ideas into practical systems. The wider space industry also includes companies working beyond rockets. Pixxel has launched six Firefly satellites that capture detailed images of Earth using hyperspectral imaging, a technology that collects information across many different wavelengths of light. Dhruva Space is developing satellite platforms and related systems. Bellatrix Aerospace is working on propulsion technologies that help spacecraft move in orbit. Digantara's SCOT satellite began operations in March 2025 to track objects orbiting Earth. GalaxEye launched its Drishti satellite on 3 May 2026, combining optical imaging with synthetic aperture radar (SAR) technology. Behind every satellite is a network of people, equipment and knowledge. Cameras, computers, electrical systems, communication links, ground stations and software all contribute to a successful mission. This creates work in electronics, manufacturing, design, testing, programming and data analysis. The space sector is therefore not limited to astronauts and rocket scientists. It also depends on people with many different skills. Space technology has practical uses in everyday life. Satellite images can help farmers understand crop conditions and researchers monitor forests, rivers and glaciers. Weather information supports preparations for storms and floods. The NASA–ISRO NISAR mission, launched in July 2025, uses radar to observe changes on Earth and support research into ecosystems, ice and natural hazards. These applications show how studying space can also help people understand and care for their home planet. Public institutions and private companies have complementary responsibilities in this developing field. ISRO contributes scientific experience, research and launch infrastructure. The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre, known as IN-SPACe, supports and authorises private-sector space activities. Private firms contribute new designs, investment and business ideas. Cooperation between research institutions, universities and industry can help make scientific knowledge useful in practical ways. Universities and research centres will remain important to this progress. Institutions such as the Indian Institutes of Technology and the Indian Institute of Science train students and support research in engineering and science. Young people can participate in this field in many ways. They may design a sensor, develop software, build a component or study satellite images. A classroom science project or a first look through a telescope can become the beginning of a lifelong interest in science. India is also preparing for human spaceflight through the Gaganyaan programme. It is developing systems intended to carry astronauts safely into space and bring them back. Its first uncrewed experimental mission will carry the half-humanoid robot Vyommitra. Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla has also visited the International Space Station, where he completed seven microgravity experiments, adding valuable experience to the country's human-spaceflight programme. In the years ahead, further developments may emerge in reusable rockets, groups of small satellites working together and robotic missions to explore the Moon and other celestial bodies. These are areas of continuing research and development. Their progress will depend on careful planning, scientific understanding, repeated testing and the responsible use of technology. Space exploration is a journey of continuous learning and progress. Every mission requires investment, specialised skills and careful preparation. Each test adds to scientific understanding, with every outcome providing valuable lessons that help engineers develop better technologies. As more objects enter orbit, advances in space monitoring and responsible practices can help make the space environment safer and more sustainable. International scientific cooperation, shared knowledge and innovation will remain important in shaping this progress. The story of space is, at its heart, a story of human curiosity, imagination and shared achievement. It is a journey that connects people everywhere through a common interest in discovering and understanding the universe. Every new discovery opens doors to further learning, while every technological advance creates possibilities for improving life on Earth. With knowledge, cooperation and a spirit of exploration, humanity can continue to move towards a future filled with discovery and opportunity. The universe remains vast, and there is still so much to learn, explore and understand. (The Author is a Columnist and can be reached at: bakshisuhaib094@gmail.com )
